name: Restraint bias
statement: People overestimate how well they can resist hunger, craving and other impulses, and that confidence leads them into temptation rather than away from it.
meaning: Nordgren, van Harreveld and van der Pligt attach the name to two linked claims. The first is that a person in a calm state rates their capacity to control hunger, fatigue or craving higher than a person currently in that state rates theirs. The second is that the belief has a cost. It makes people accept more exposure to temptation, and the exposure then produces the impulsive act. So the claim is about a belief and its behavioural consequence, rather than about a preference shifting under arousal. That second idea is the hot-cold empathy gap, which has its own entry here, no. 166, and its own evidence. The word bias carries an accuracy claim, because a belief can only be called inflated against some standard of what a person's control actually is. The four published studies compare beliefs held in a hot state against beliefs held in a cold state. None of them tests a belief against the control its holder turns out to have. The thesis version reports that comparison for the cafeteria study, and the published article leaves it out.

origin.who: Loran F. Nordgren, Frenk van Harreveld and Joop van der Pligt
origin.note: The paper ran in volume 20, issue 12, pages 1523 to 1528, was received on 28 February 2009 and accepted in revision on 21 April 2009. It coins the term and reports four studies. An earlier three-study version appears as chapter 5 of Nordgren's 2008 Amsterdam doctoral thesis, credited there to Nordgren, van der Pligt and van Harreveld and marked under review. Its second study is a sexual-arousal experiment that does not appear in the published paper, and the published paper's two smoker studies do not appear in it.

evidence: Study 1 gave 72 Amsterdam students a memory task lasting about 20 minutes or a two-minute version of the same task. The long version left them more fatigued, 5.17 against 3.87 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 70) = 41.84, p < .001, eta squared .34. Fatigued students then rated their control over mental fatigue lower, 5.09 against 5.60, F(1, 70) = 8.17, p = .005, eta squared .09, and planned to leave less of next semester's studying to the final week, 52.68% against 59.38%, F(1, 70) = 4.51, p = .04, eta squared .05. Study 2 was a field experiment at a cafeteria. Seventy-nine people ranked seven snacks, chose one, and were told they would earn four euros and keep the snack if they brought it back uneaten a week later. People entering the cafeteria were hungrier than people leaving, 4.88 against 2.43, and rated their control over hunger lower, 4.32 against 4.91, F(1, 77) = 6.86, p = .01, eta squared .08. The satiated picked a more tempting snack, mean rank 6.21 against 5.47, F(1, 77) = 10.76, p = .002, eta squared .12, and stronger control beliefs went with a more tempting choice, r(79) = .35, p = .002. Thirty-nine snacks came back. The return rate was 60.5% in the hungry condition against 39.0% in the satiated one, which the paper reports as not reaching significance, chi-square(1, N = 79) = 3.65, p = .06. Study 3 gave 53 student smokers a bogus implicit test and told half of them they had a high capacity for impulse control and half that they had a low one. They then watched a film for money, choosing how close a cigarette would be: in another room for two euros, on the desk for four, in their hand for six, in their mouth for eight. High-control smokers chose closer, 3.00 against 2.38, F(1, 51) = 5.54, p = .02, eta squared .09, and 33.33% of them smoked during the film against 11.52% of the low-control group, chi-square(1, N = 51) = 3.59, p = .06. Study 4 followed 55 smokers who had been abstinent for three weeks in a cessation programme. Those with stronger impulse-control beliefs reported avoiding smoking cues less, r(55) = -.32, p = .02, and less avoidance predicted heavier smoking four months later, beta = -.76, SE = .29, t(55) = -2.61, p = .01. About a third of the sample, 32.71%, were still abstinent at follow-up.

examples.tag: The biscuit tin on the desk
examples.text: Just after lunch, someone agrees to keep the office biscuits beside the keyboard, certain they can be ignored. The confidence was formed while full, and what it decided was how much temptation the afternoon would contain.

examples.tag: The quitter who keeps going to the pub
examples.text: A fortnight into stopping smoking, a man carries on meeting friends who smoke, on the grounds that the hard part is behind him. The belief shows up first as less avoidance, and that is the step the claim is clearest about.

examples.tag: An hour in the shops to prove a point
examples.text: Someone saving for a deposit browses the shops on a free afternoon to show the budget is under control. Judging one's own restraint from a calm moment is what arranges the exposure that tests it.

replication.headline: No replication of any of the four studies was found. What independent scrutiny exists is a statistical audit, which concluded that the four results are too uniformly successful for their own sample sizes.
replication.detail: Gregory Francis applied his test of excess success to every Psychological Science article from 2009 to 2012 that reported four or more experiments, and this paper is one of them. Using the effect sizes and sample sizes the paper itself reports, he estimated the probability that each study would come out as it did: .545, .518, .531 and .667. Francis calls all four upper limits, because each study ran further tests whose joint power he could not estimate. Multiplied together they give a joint probability of .0998, below his .1 criterion, so the analysis says readers should be sceptical that the reported pattern reflects the theory. His supplementary note also records the paper's inconsistent handling of its own threshold, since Studies 2 and 3 report the same p value of .06 and the paper calls one non-significant and the other significant. The test is contested. Van Boxtel and Koch argue that Francis's verdicts turn on which experiments and which significance tests he groups together. They mark 34 of the 44 articles as open to that objection, this one among them, and say plainly that they did not test whether a different choice would change any verdict. Their own p-curve, run on all 44 articles, found evidential value in 9, inadequate evidential value in 11 and a p-hacking signal in 1. For this article it returned none of the three, at p values of .54, .19 and .46, with the aggregate power of the tests below 5%. An audit is not a replication, and a joint probability of .0998 against a threshold of .1 is a verdict with very little margin.

limits: Nothing in the paper establishes that anyone overestimated anything. Each study compares beliefs in a hot state against beliefs in a cold state, and calling the cold figure inflated assumes the hot figure is correct. Nordgren's thesis says so directly, though of its first two studies rather than all of them: from that evidence alone the accuracy of people's estimates cannot be established, and the aroused participants might equally have been underestimating themselves. The thesis then presents the cafeteria study as the one that does address accuracy, and reports there that people who returned the snack held weaker control beliefs than people who did not, at p = .04. That comparison is absent from the published article. The behavioural results are thin. The snack return difference in Study 2 was p = .06, the smoking difference in Study 3 was p = .06, and in Study 4 impulse-control beliefs were not related to smoking status at all, a correlation of .16 the paper marks as not significant. Study 2 was not randomised, which the authors give as a limitation, and Study 4 recruited only smokers who had already lasted three weeks, which they also flag. Cell sizes run from 26 to 41. Study 3 describes 53 participants and then reports every test on 51. Study 1 prints standard deviations of 1.32 and 1.50 for percentages whose means are 52.68 and 59.38. The copy read for this entry is the publisher's typeset file rather than a scan, and it prints the minus signs on r(55) = -.32 and on beta = -.76. Its embedded fonts defeat text extraction, which turns equals signs into fives and drops those minus signs, so a figure copied out of the file can arrive pointing the wrong way. Nearby work points the other way. Gwaltney, Metrik, Kahler and Shiffman reviewed 54 prospective studies of smoking cessation and found that confidence in one's ability to abstain went with better outcomes, by .21 standard deviations when measured before a quit attempt and .28 when measured among people already abstinent, which is Study 4's design. That .28 rests on 20 studies and comes to about 2% of the variance in outcome, and the authors call the relationship reliable but less robust than expected. Their construct is abstinence self-efficacy rather than impulse-control belief, so the two are not interchangeable. Witt, Raggio, Butryn and Lowe gave 67 people a standard meal and a four-hour fast, then randomised them to a protein shake or none and to the sight of palatable food or none. They found no effect on self-reported hedonic hunger, external eating or disinhibition, with all effect sizes at partial eta squared of .015 or below. Those scales are not the impulse-control measure used here. The search for replications was run again on 21 September 2026. PubMed indexes one item for the phrase, the paper itself. Semantic Scholar lists 33 citing papers and no title among them is a replication. OpenAlex counts 111 citing works, but its listing endpoint refused the request that day, so that list was not read. Crossref and web searches pairing the term with replication, preregistration and OSF turned up nothing. Europe PMC's search service returned empty results and server errors, so its citation list was not re-read. PsycINFO and Web of Science were not searched. No direct or conceptual replication was found, and no meta-analysis.
misreadings: The paper's own abstract reports a chain the data do not close: that inflated beliefs led recovering smokers to more temptation, which led to higher relapse four months later. The two links were tested separately and only one held. Beliefs predicted less avoidance, avoidance predicted relapse, and beliefs did not predict relapse. No mediation test for that chain appears in Study 4. Popular retellings compress it further into the claim that confident quitters relapse more, which is the correlation the paper reports as null. The second common error is to treat the studies as demonstrations of overconfidence. They show that hot and cold participants answer differently, which is a difference, not an error. The third is to read Study 2 as an experiment. People were approached entering or leaving a cafeteria, so hunger was measured rather than assigned, and the authors say they cannot rule out other differences between the two groups. Study 3's smoking result, 33.33% against 11.52%, is often quoted as the clean causal demonstration. Its p value is .06, and the paper calls that difference significant while calling an identical p value in Study 2 non-significant. The restraint bias is also treated as another name for the hot-cold empathy gap. It is a further claim built on top of it, about what beliefs about self-control do to behaviour, and the empathy gap's evidence does not carry over.

sources.text: Nordgren, L. F., van Harreveld, F., & van der Pligt, J. (2009). The restraint bias: How the illusion of self-restraint promotes impulsive behavior. Psychological Science, 20(12), 1523-1528. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the publisher's typeset PDF, posted on a university course page; every figure quoted above is from that text, and the minus signs on r = -.32 and beta = -.76 are printed on the page.

Nordgren, L. F. (2008). Thinking about feeling: The nature and significance of the hot/cold empathy gap. Doctoral thesis, University of Amsterdam. Chapter 5 is the earlier three-study version of the paper, read in full on 21 September 2026; source of the 91 people approached at the cafeteria, the dropped sexual-arousal study of 60 men recruited and 54 analysed, the statement that accuracy cannot be established from the first two studies, and the comparison of control beliefs by snack return that the published article omits.

Francis, G. (2014). The frequency of excess success for articles in Psychological Science. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 21(5), 1180-1187. The analysis of this paper is section 42 and Table S43 of the supplementary material, downloaded from the author's Purdue page on 21 September 2026 and read in full; source of the four success probabilities, which Francis calls upper limits, and of PTES = .0998.

van Boxtel, J. J. A., & Koch, C. (2016). Reevaluating excess success in psychological science. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 23(5), 1602-1606. Read in full on 21 September 2026, with its supplementary Table S1, from rd.springer.com, which served the PDF that link.springer.com answered with a bot challenge; source of the 34 of 44 figure, the p-curve counts and this article's own p-curve values.

Gwaltney, C. J., Metrik, J., Kahler, C. W., & Shiffman, S. (2009). Self-efficacy and smoking cessation: A meta-analysis. Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, 23(1), 56-66. Read in full on 21 September 2026 as the author manuscript deposited at PubMed Central, fetched through the NCBI eutils route after the rendered page served a captcha; the manuscript carries the published title, authors, journal and DOI. Source of the 54 studies, the .21, .47 and .28 standard-deviation figures and the 2% of variance.

Witt, A. A., Raggio, G. A., Butryn, M. L., & Lowe, M. R. (2014). Do hunger and exposure to food affect scores on a measure of hedonic hunger? An experimental study. Appetite, 74, 1-5. Abstract read in full on 21 September 2026 from the PubMed record, for the sample of 67, the design, the null results and the effect-size ceiling. Unpaywall lists no open full text, and none was found.

Nordgren, L. F., & Chou, E. Y. (2011). The push and pull of temptation: The bidirectional influence of temptation on self-control. Psychological Science, 22(11), 1386-1390. The same lab's follow-up, in which temptation prompts self-control in a cold state and impulsive behaviour in a hot one. Abstract read on 21 September 2026 from the PubMed record; not a replication of the 2009 studies, and Unpaywall lists no open full text.
